conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s a brief, 10-question screen that helps us see whether you might be experiencing any symptoms of depression, anxiety, or distress that sometimes crop up in the weeks after birth. Everything you share stays confidential between you and our team, and my goal is simply to understand how you’re doing so we can offer the best support possible.

We’ll go through the questions one at a time, focusing on how you’ve felt over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. Ready to start?

First question: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Sometimes I can—like when my baby makes those little faces while sleeping—but most of the time I just feel too tired to find things funny. Even when my partner jokes around, I’ll smile, but the laughter doesn’t come easily.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes… I’ve been able to laugh a little, but it’s not like before. Mostly I have to remind myself to, and it feels kind of forced.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to—like when my mom offers to watch the baby so I can take a walk or grab coffee—but the excitement fizzles out fast. I still go, but it feels more like I’m doing it because I “should,” not because I truly look forward to it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday he spit up a ton right after I fed him, and even though the nurse said it’s normal, I kept thinking maybe I held him wrong or ate something that upset his stomach. It’s not constant, but little stuff like that makes me wonder if I’m messing up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there while the baby’s asleep and suddenly my heart starts racing—like, what if his breathing sounds weird or what if the crib suddenly collapses? Nothing’s actually wrong, but the thoughts just pop in and I can’t shake them right away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It’s happened a few times—like this tight, shaky feeling out of nowhere. Last night I was rocking the baby in the dark and suddenly pictured him not breathing. My chest got heavy, I had to turn on all the lights and check him over and over. It passed after a minute, but it left me jittery for a while.
Things have been getting on top of me
Some of the time. I keep thinking I should be able to juggle the feeds, the laundry, a shower… but then the day slips away and I feel like I’m barely treading water. I manage, but it’s tiring.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—mostly just keyed-up and worried. I’ll lie down once the baby’s out, but my brain keeps replaying every little grunt or hiccup I heard on the monitor. Takes me a long time to settle, then I jolt awake if he makes the tiniest noise.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do feel that way off and on—not all day, but it hits me in waves. Like yesterday afternoon everything just felt heavy and gray for a couple of hours, then it eased up after I got outside for a bit.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I’ve teared up once or twice—like when I couldn’t get him to latch and felt useless—but actual crying hasn’t happened. Mostly I just feel tense or numb instead.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’m tired and overwhelmed sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy: laughter comes only with effort, excitement fades quickly, and waves of worry or sadness catch you off-guard. Even when you know many of these concerns aren't grounded in real danger, your body still races and your mind circles around <sym>what-ifs</sym>. You're working hard to care for your baby and meet daily demands, yet you often feel you're <quote>barely treading water</quote>.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh, describing it as forced and requiring conscious effort, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient still attempts activities but reports that any enjoyment quickly fades and participation feels obligatory, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "some of the time" with specific examples, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes with intrusive catastrophic imagery and persistent jitteriness, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>"Some of the time" aligns with "sometimes" in option 2; she reports struggling to keep up with daily tasks yet still managing, indicating intermittent difficulty coping.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports significant sleep disruption driven by anxious hyper-vigilance about the baby, aligning with "Yes, sometimes" even though she denies feeling "unhappy" per se.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intermittent sadness that comes "in waves," occurring "off and on" and lasting hours, aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 18 places you well above the 14-point cutoff that signals probable major depressive or anxiety disorder in the perinatal period. You endorsed <sym>daily unprovoked anxiety</sym> (Q4=3), frequent <sym>panic sensations</sym> (Q5=2), and persistent difficulty looking forward to activities (Q2=2), all of which align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety disorders</med>. Although you denied suicidal thoughts (Q10=0), the combined mood and anxiety burden still warrants prompt clinical attention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary-care physician</med> to review these results
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for fuller assessment and to discuss evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>sertraline</med>, both compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan brief daily self-check-ins: note mood, anxiety level, and any new thoughts of self-harm; share these notes at your appointment
4. Encourage 20-30 minutes of gentle outdoor activity (walk with stroller, sit on porch) once a day; daylight can modestly improve <sym>mood</sym> and <sym>sleep</sym>
5. Stagger visitors so you have at least one quiet block for rest; enlist partner or family to handle a night feeding so you can get a 4-5 hour stretch of sleep
6. Limit Googling symptoms; instead write worries in a notebook and set a 10-minute <quote>worry window</quote> later to reduce bedtime rumination
7. Keep follow-up EPDS in two weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen or any thoughts of self-harm emerge; call emergency services if you ever feel unsafe
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant age not stated)  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [your name, LPC/LCSW]

Presenting Symptoms  
- Anhedonia: reports diminished ability to laugh or look forward to activities; participation feels “forced.”  
- Episodic low mood: describes waves of sadness/misery lasting hours, improved transiently by distraction.  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame: attributes normal infant behaviors (e.g., spit-up) to maternal error.  
- Generalized anxiety: daily racing heart, catastrophic worries about infant safety without objective trigger.  
- Panic-like episodes: sudden chest tightness, visualizing infant not breathing, repeated checking compulsively.  
- Sleep disturbance: difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep when infant is quiet; hyper-arousal related to monitor sounds.  
- Feeling overwhelmed: endorses “things getting on top of me,” difficulty completing daily tasks.  
- No suicidal or self-harm ideation (explicitly denied).  

Patterns / Risk Indicators  
Mood and anxiety symptoms co-occur; functional impairment evident in self-care and task completion. No current safety concerns.

Screening Impression  
Meets threshold for possible postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety. Recommend formal clinical interview (EPDS or PHQ-9; GAD-7) and referral to OB/primary-care or perinatal mental health specialist for evaluation and treatment planning.
